title: Is one product of primes a multiple or a factor of another?
description: Two numbers are given as products of primes. Counting each prime shows that the first is not a multiple of the second and not a factor of the second. The answer is checked with the actual numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: a multiple must hold all the primes of the other number, and a factor can use no prime more often than the other number does. Ask the class to count the primes of both numbers before the working is shown. Watch for students who only compare the sizes of the two numbers.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q2
video_script.why: The child has compared prime counts to find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple and now uses the same counts to decide when one number is a multiple or a factor of another.
video_script.substitution: Count each prime in both numbers, then compare the counts for a multiple and for a factor.
video_script.anchor: The two products of primes written one under the other, with the same primes in the same columns.
video_script.payoff_line: The answer to both questions is no
maths_rules: counts of the first: 5 once, 7 once, 11 twice; counts of the second: 2 once, 5 once, 7 twice, 11 once
a multiple of the second must have a 2 and two 7s; the first has no 2, so it is not a multiple
a factor of the second can have 11 only once; the first has two 11s, so it is not a factor
check: multiples of 5390 start at 5390, above 4235; multiples of 4235 are 4235 and 8470, and 5390 lies between them
video_script.design: One idea: compare the prime counts of the two numbers. The two products of primes stay on the board and the counts that break each condition are lit.
